pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 1: Growing: nothing. Waiting: everything.*

I would like to say I found the garden because I am curious and brave. What actually happened is that I was hiding from a stack of moving boxes.

Lowell Court is eleven concrete blocks around a car park, and I had been living in Block C for nine days, which is enough time to know exactly how long the lift takes (forty seconds, if it feels like it) and how many steps lead up to our flat on the fourth floor (ninety-two), and not nearly enough time to know a single person. The blocks are the color of old chewing gum. The car park has one tree, and the tree has a fence around it, as if it might try something.

I am Sana Haddad. I am eleven. I have round glasses, a green pencil that lives in my hair, and a serious problem with waiting, which I did not know was a problem until I moved somewhere with nothing else to do.
pages.image: Sana, a thin 11-year-old girl with brown skin, round glasses and a low black bun with a green pencil through it, stands in a grey concrete car park surrounded by tall drab apartment blocks, holding a moving box and looking up with a slightly dismayed face; one small fenced tree stands alone nearby.

pages.text:
Our flat was full of boxes. Mama, who is a night nurse, was asleep in the middle of the day with a pillow over her head and a sign on the door that said IF YOU WAKE ME, YOU BECOME THE PATIENT. Baba, who is a baker, had left at three in the morning and would be home at noon with a bag of warm bread and flour in his eyebrows. My brother Yusuf, who is six and has not yet lost the habit of speaking at the volume of a fire alarm, was explaining to the empty living room exactly how a dinosaur would carry a sofa.

I wanted the flat to feel like home. I wanted this by Friday. I had made a list of what needed to happen, and unpacking was only the first line. The other lines said things like *know where the bus goes* and *have one friend*.

It was Tuesday. I had unpacked four boxes and I had not yet found the kettle.
pages.image: A crowded flat full of cardboard boxes; Mama, a tired woman in blue nurse's scrubs, sleeps on a sofa with a pillow over her head; Yusuf, a small boy with missing front teeth, stands on a box waving his arms in a lively explanation, and Sana stands in the doorway holding a list

pages.text:
Here is the proof that I am not a patient person. Four days earlier I had pushed a bean into a yogurt cup of soil on the windowsill, and I had checked it every hour since with a ruler.

Nothing had happened. Nothing usually does, for the first week. I knew this. I had read it in a library book called *Beans: A Beginner's Guide*. But knowing a thing and being able to leave it alone are two different animals, and on the third night I had dug the bean up with a teaspoon to make sure it was working. It was working. It had a small pale root, like a whisker. I had put it back and felt terrible, and the following morning I had done it again.

The bean now looked slightly offended. I understood the feeling.

"You are not being helpful," I told it.

The bean, as beans do, said nothing at all.
pages.image: Sana, in an oversized denim jacket, leans over a windowsill measuring a yogurt cup of soil with a ruler, frowning at it with great concentration; a teaspoon lies beside the cup and afternoon light comes through the window over the grey estate outside.

pages.text:
The lift was out of order, so I took the stairs, and on the second landing I met Mr. Osei.

Mr. Osei is the caretaker of Lowell Court. He is very tall and very quiet and has a grey moustache and a ring of keys on his belt as big as a dinner plate, and he mops the same six square meters of lift floor every morning as if he were painting it. That day he was leaning on his mop looking at nothing in particular. He nodded at me. I nodded at him. We had done this eleven times already, and I was keeping count.

"The bean," he said, unexpectedly, "will not grow any faster for being looked at."

I opened my mouth to ask how he knew about the bean. Then I remembered that everybody in Block C knew everything about everybody's windowsills.

"I know that," I said. I did not.

He gave me a long, mild look. Then his eyes went past me, out through the stair window toward the loading bay at the back of the block, and something crossed his face that I did not have a name for yet. He went back to mopping.
pages.image: Mr. Osei, a very tall soft-spoken man with a grey moustache, blue overalls and a huge ring of keys, leans on a mop on a concrete stair landing and gives Sana a long gentle look; through the window behind him a loading bay and a strip of chain-link fence are visible.

pages.text:
I meant to go straight up to the flat. I really did. But there were the boxes waiting for me, and the list, and Yusuf's dinosaur, and I could not face any of it, so I went down instead, and out, and round the back of the block to the loading bay, where nobody ever goes.

It smelled of bins and diesel and old rain. There was a row of overflowing bins, a broken pigeon feeder, and a chain-link fence along the far edge, where the pavement stopped and the world seemed to give up. I was about to turn back when I noticed two things. The first was that the bottom of the fence had been pulled up, just enough to fit a person, if the person was small and did not mind mud.

The second was the smell. It was very faint, and completely wrong for the place: wet earth and mint and something like lemons, thick and green and alive, drifting through the gap like a whisper that had been waiting for someone to lean in.

I looked back at the bins. Then I got down on my hands and knees and crawled through.
pages.image: Sana on her hands and knees crawling under a pulled-up section of chain-link fence behind a grey concrete loading bay, looking through the gap toward a glimpse of vivid green leaves, with bins and concrete blocks behind her.
